rationale: Schizophrenia reliably shows a slower individual alpha rhythm. Relative band power with a fixed 8–13 Hz band can only partly capture that shift, so I'm adding a per-channel alpha centre-of-gravity frequency (7–14 Hz, from the Welch PSD). It doesn't depend on amplitude scale or recording length, which helps when the model is applied to the external datasets.

The recordings have had no artifact rejection, so the PSD is currently a mean over 2-s Welch segments, and a few blink, movement or muscle bursts can dominate the delta and gamma bands. I'm switching Welch to median averaging across segments, which down-weights those bursts. The resulting relative band power should better reflect the background EEG (where the schizophrenia markers are: more slow-wave activity, less alpha). It should also hold up better on the shorter, noisier external recordings.

I'm adding the aperiodic (1/f) slope for each channel. It is fit as a log-log line over 2–40 Hz, leaving out the 7–14 Hz alpha peak. Schizophrenia has been linked to a changed excitation/inhibition balance, and the slope is thought to reflect that balance. Band power alone mixes the slope in with oscillatory changes. The slope doesn't depend on amplitude scale, so it should carry over to the external amplifiers. This is untested so far.

I'm adding one feature family, the per-channel aperiodic (1/f) exponent. It is the slope of log power against log frequency, fitted over 2–7 Hz and 14–40 Hz so the alpha peak and line noise are left out of the fit. Schizophrenia is linked to a changed excitation/inhibition balance, and that shows up as a changed 1/f slope. Relative band power misses it because it mixes periodic and aperiodic power. The slope also doesn't change with amplitude scale, which helps on the external sets.

The recordings have had no artifact rejection, so the mean-averaged Welch PSD can be dominated by a few windows with eye blinks, movement or electrode pops. These mainly inflate delta and total power, which distorts the relative band powers. This change switches Welch to median averaging across windows, a simple robust way to suppress transient artifacts. It should also travel better to the external clinics, where artifact load will be different.

I'm splitting alpha into 8–10/10–13 Hz and beta into 13–20/20–30 Hz. Schizophrenia often shows slower alpha (power moving from upper to lower alpha) and changes in lower vs upper beta, and the single wide alpha and beta bands average those shifts away. Relative power keeps the features unaffected by amplitude scale, which matters for the external datasets. I haven't run this, so I don't know its dev score yet.

I'm adding one per-channel aperiodic (1/f) exponent to the existing log relative band powers. It's a robust log-log fit of the spectrum over 2–40 Hz that leaves out the alpha range (7–14 Hz). Schizophrenia has been linked to a flatter or steeper aperiodic slope, which is thought to reflect the balance of neural excitation and inhibition. Band power alone mixes this background slope with real oscillations. The exponent doesn't change with amplitude scale, so it should carry over to the external amplifiers. I haven't run this version, so its Dev score is unknown.

The recordings have no artifact rejection, so a few blink, movement or electrode-pop segments can inflate the mean-averaged Welch PSD and skew relative band power. Averaging the PSD with the median across 2-s segments (`average='median'`) is more robust to those artifacts. It should give a cleaner spectral biomarker (e.g. the delta/theta increase and alpha decrease seen in SZ) and transfer better to the external clinics.

I'm adding one aperiodic (1/f) exponent per channel to the existing relative band powers. It's a log-log linear fit of the Welch PSD over 2–40 Hz, leaving out the alpha peak (7–14 Hz). Schizophrenia is linked to a changed excitation/inhibition balance, which shows up as a different 1/f slope. The slope doesn't depend on amplitude scale, so it should hold up on the external amplifiers. I haven't run this, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

I'm adding two spectral-shape markers that the literature links to schizophrenia and that relative band power can't fully capture. The first is the per-channel aperiodic (1/f) exponent, fitted in log-log space over 2–40 Hz with the alpha range (7–14 Hz) left out, which is thought to reflect the brain's excitation/inhibition balance. The second is the posterior individual alpha peak frequency, which tends to be slower in schizophrenia. Both are unaffected by amplitude scale and recording length, so they should carry over to the external MSU/RepOD sets.

The recordings have had no artifact rejection, so a few seconds of eye movement, muscle or electrode-pop activity can inflate the mean-averaged Welch PSD and distort relative band power. This version uses a median across the 2-s Welch segments instead of the mean. That is a simple way to reject artifacts per segment, and it should make the spectral biomarker (more slow-wave power, less alpha in schizophrenia) more stable within ASEEG and on the external MSU/RepOD recordings, which are of differing quality.

The recordings have had no artifact rejection, so a few blinks, movement or muscle bursts can skew the mean Welch PSD. I'm switching Welch to median averaging across segments (`average="median"`), which gives a robust per-channel spectrum without dropping any data. This should make the relative band powers reflect the true resting spectrum more closely, and it should also hold up on the short, noisy 1-minute external recordings.

Schizophrenia is linked to a changed excitation/inhibition balance, which shows up as a different aperiodic (1/f) exponent in the EEG spectrum. This change adds a per-channel 1/f exponent, fitted to the log-log Welch PSD over 2–40 Hz with the alpha band (7–14 Hz) and line-noise frequencies left out. The exponent does not depend on amplitude scale, so it should also carry over to external amplifiers; the relative band-power features stay as they are. This has not been run yet, so there is no Dev score for it.

I'm switching the Welch PSD from mean to median averaging across 2-s segments. The recordings have had no artifact rejection, so a few eye-movement, muscle or electrode-pop segments can inflate delta and gamma power when segments are averaged. The median gives a cleaner estimate of each subject's background spectrum, which should help both the dev score and transfer to the external clinics' recordings.

Schizophrenia reliably shows slowing of the dominant alpha rhythm (lower individual alpha frequency), and fixed 8–13 Hz band powers only partly capture this. This change adds a per-channel alpha centre-of-gravity frequency (7–13 Hz) computed from the same Welch PSD. The new feature is unaffected by amplitude scale and recording length, which matters for MSU and RepOD.

Schizophrenia is linked to a slower individual alpha peak and a changed aperiodic (1/f) exponent. Relative band power with fixed band edges captures neither cleanly, so I add two per-channel features from the same Welch PSD: the alpha centre-of-gravity frequency and the log-log aperiodic slope (fitted over 2–40 Hz, excluding the 7–14 Hz alpha range). Neither feature depends on amplitude scale, which matters for the external sets.

In schizophrenia the resting alpha rhythm slows: power moves from upper alpha (10–13 Hz) into lower alpha (8–10 Hz) and theta, and delta/theta power rises. The current 5 broad bands average over that shift. This round I split them into 8 narrower bands (low/high theta, low/high alpha, low/high beta) so the regularized logistic regression can see it. The features stay as log relative power, so they remain insensitive to amplitude scale across clinics and amplifiers.

Schizophrenia is linked to slower alpha (power shifting from the upper to the lower alpha range) and to extra power in the lower theta range. The current five broad bands blur these effects together. This change splits theta, alpha and beta into lower and upper sub-bands, so the scale-invariant relative-power features can pick up spectral slowing, while the same log-relative, standardized, L2 logistic regression setup is kept.

The 5 canonical bands blur together the spectral changes reported in schizophrenia: a slower alpha peak, a shift of power into the alpha1 versus alpha2 sub-bands, and excess delta/theta. Each band ratio is still relative, so the features stay scale-invariant for the external sets. This change replaces the 5 bands with log relative power in 22 narrow 2-Hz bins (1–45 Hz) per channel. Because that gives many more features, the regularization strength C is now chosen by inner grouped CV on the training fold only.

I'm adding one per-channel feature: the individual alpha frequency, computed as the power-weighted mean frequency between 7 and 13 Hz. People with schizophrenia tend to have a slower alpha peak, and fixed 8–13 Hz band-power bins don't capture that well. The feature also doesn't change with amplitude scale or recording length, which should help on the external sets. Everything else stays the same.
